session: 2026 Oklahoma Legislative Session (adjourned sine die mid-May 2026)

bills.title: Data Center Consumer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026
bills.lastAction: In effect as of July 1, 2026. Signed by Gov. Stitt in May 2026. Requires large-load customers (75+ MW) to pay for new grid infrastructure, mandates separate tariffs with credit requirements, and requires developers to notify the Corporation Commission, county commissioners, and neighboring property owners within 60 days of buying land for a project.
bills.policyRelevance: Ensures data center operators bear proportional costs for grid infrastructure upgrades rather than passing them to residential ratepayers. Defines large-load customers as 75+ MW facilities. Now the tariff framework the Oklahoma Corporation Commission must apply to the first live loads. Covered in depth in Issue #17 (The Meter Goes Live) and Issue #19 (The Gate).

bills.title: Data Center Groundwater Protection Act
bills.lastAction: Signed by Gov. Stitt May 20, 2026. Final language defines penalties for failure to report groundwater usage, requires data centers to use closed-loop cooling systems to qualify for a groundwater usage permit, protects users who draw less than their permitted amount from allocation reductions, and creates a complaint process through the Oklahoma Water Resources Board.
bills.policyRelevance: The water-side companion to HB 2992's cost-attribution floor: metering and closed-loop cooling for large-load data centers. Of direct relevance to Phoenix Wells and geothermal procurement, since enhanced geothermal does not consume the cooling-tower water cycle most hyperscale data centers rely on. Covered in Issue #15 (Water on the Meter).

bills.title: Oklahoma Computer Data Privacy Act
bills.lastAction: Signed into law in March 2026. House passed 84-4.
bills.policyRelevance: Oklahoma's first comprehensive consumer data privacy law, joining roughly twenty states with comprehensive frameworks: gives residents rights over personal data collection, sale, and deletion by companies.

bills.title: Oklahoma Responsible Technology in Schools Act
bills.lastAction: Approved by Governor May 12, 2026, with emergency clause. Requires every district to adopt a written AI policy before the 2027-28 school year; mandates educator-directed, human-in-the-loop AI use; prohibits AI as the primary basis for grading, discipline, or placement; preserves parents' right to opt students out of student-facing AI tools without academic penalty.
bills.policyRelevance: Sets a statewide floor for AI governance in K-12: district policies, human oversight, a ban on high-stakes AI decisions, and family transparency. One of the first state frameworks of its kind.

bills.title: Crimes and punishments; modifying elements of certain unlawful acts; aggravated identity theft; effective date
bills.lastAction: Became law without the Governor's signature on May 7, 2026. Takes effect November 1, 2026. Creates aggravated identity theft and makes it a crime to use a stolen or made-up (synthetic) identity, with intent to defraud, to get money or property. Anyone who uses artificial intelligence, among other digital tools, to commit identity theft faces additional penalties on top of the identity theft charge.
bills.policyRelevance: With SB 1734, one of the AI-related bills that became Oklahoma law in 2026. It does not regulate AI itself; it names AI as a tool of identity theft and raises the penalty for using it that way.

bills.title: Minor Protection from AI (Conversational AI Services)
bills.lastAction: Passed the Senate 43-0 on March 23, 2026. The House passed an amended version 90-0 on April 28 and sent it back to the Senate on April 29. The Legislature ended its session on May 14 before the Senate voted on the House changes, so the bill died. It does not carry over; it would have to be refiled in 2027. Correction, October 26, 2026: this entry said the bill was enacted. It was not.
bills.policyRelevance: No legislator voted against it in either chamber, and it still died: the calendar ran out, not the votes. The House's version would have required operators of AI chat services used by minors to provide parental controls and to send users who mention self-harm to crisis services.

bills.title: Chatbot Safety for Minors Act
bills.lastAction: Passed the House but did not complete the process before sine die adjournment in mid-May. Its Senate counterpart, SB 1521, also died at adjournment. Bills not enacted by the end of the 2026 session (the second session of the 60th Legislature) are dead and do not carry over.
bills.policyRelevance: House companion to SB 1521. Neither became law in 2026.

bills.title: Affordable, Reliable, Clean Energy Security Act
bills.lastAction: Did not advance out of committee before sine die adjournment in mid-May 2026. Dead for this legislature; the ARC framework would need to be refiled in 2027.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have established affordable, reliable, clean energy security as state policy priorities with reliability standards and domestic-sourcing preferences. Watch for a 2027 refile.

bills.title: Well Repurposing Act
bills.lastAction: Passed House 85-6 but stuck on Senate general order calendar. Did not advance by the May 7 opposite-chamber deadline. Dead for the 2026 session and does not carry over.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have converted abandoned oil and gas wells into geothermal energy sources. Strong House support but no Senate floor vote before deadline. Directly relevant to Phoenix Wells; a 2027 refile is the path forward.

bills.title: Data Center Energy Surcharge Act
bills.lastAction: Did not advance out of the House Energy & Natural Resources Committee before sine die adjournment in mid-May 2026.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have imposed an energy surcharge on large data centers consuming above a threshold. The cost-attribution ground it aimed at was partly covered by HB 2992, which did become law.

bills.title: AI-Generated Deepfake Disclosure Act
bills.lastAction: Did not advance out of Senate Judiciary Committee before sine die adjournment in mid-May 2026.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have required disclosure labeling on AI-generated deepfake content in political advertising and public communications. Expect the topic to return in 2027 ahead of the election cycle.

bills.title: Deepfake Election Integrity Act
bills.lastAction: Did not advance out of the House Elections & Ethics Committee before sine die adjournment in mid-May 2026.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have criminalized distribution of AI-generated deepfakes intended to influence elections within 90 days of an election. Likely to be refiled as 2027 approaches the midterm cycle.

bills.title: Insurance Algorithm Transparency Act
bills.lastAction: Did not advance out of the Senate Insurance Committee before sine die adjournment in mid-May 2026.
bills.policyRelevance: Would have required insurers to disclose AI algorithm use in rate-setting and claims decisions, with a consumer appeals process.
